# Additional Resources {#sec-resources}

This appendix points to external resources for topics that go deeper than what this book covers. The selections here are oriented toward public health practitioners building data science skills in R, with emphasis on free and openly available material.

Nearly everything listed here is free. @sec-trainingbudget covers the separate question of what to buy when you have a professional development budget and a deadline.

## Learning R

**[R for Data Science](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/)** (Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Grolemund) is the standard starting point for learning the tidyverse. It covers data import, transformation with dplyr, visualization with ggplot2, and the broader workflow of doing data analysis in R. The second edition is freely available online. Most DSTT participants will benefit from working through at least the first half.

**[What They Forgot to Teach You About R](https://rstats.wtf/)** (Bryan and Hester) covers working in R effectively: project-oriented workflows, path discipline, R startup files, and the habits that separate reproducible work from fragile one-off scripts. Short and practical.

**[The tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org/)** documents naming conventions, spacing, and code organization conventions used across the tidyverse. Following a consistent style makes code easier to read, review, and maintain. The [`styler`](https://styler.r-lib.org/) package can apply many of these rules automatically.

## Going Deeper in R

**[Advanced R](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/)** (Wickham) covers R's object systems, functional programming, metaprogramming, and performance. It is aimed at people who already use R regularly and want to understand why things work the way they do, write more expressive code, and debug problems that go beyond "my package isn't loading."

**[R Packages](https://r-pkgs.org/)** (Wickham and Bryan) is the definitive guide to writing R packages. A package is the right container for analysis code that needs to be shared across projects or team members. It bundles functions, documentation, and tests in a standardized way that makes everything easier to reuse. Even teams that do not plan to publish to CRAN benefit from the structure packages impose. This book walks through the complete workflow using `devtools` and `usethis`.

**[Mastering Shiny](https://mastering-shiny.org/)** (Wickham) covers building interactive web applications with Shiny. Shiny apps require a running R process (unlike Quarto dashboards) but support interactivity such as user-driven filtering, on-the-fly modeling, custom inputs. This book covers reactive programming, app architecture, and deployment.

## Visualization

**[ggplot2: Elegant Graphics for Data Analysis](https://ggplot2-book.org/)** (Wickham, Navarro, and Pedersen) goes beyond the basics of `geom_*` functions to cover the grammar of graphics underlying ggplot2, how to extend it, and how to build custom themes and scales. Useful for teams that produce a lot of publication-quality figures and want consistent, polished output.

**[R Graphics Cookbook](https://r-graphics.org/)** (Chang) is organized as a collection of recipes: a problem followed by a solution. Less conceptual than the ggplot2 book, more useful as a quick reference when you know what you want a plot to look like but not how to produce it.

**[Storytelling with Data](https://www.storytellingwithdata.com/)** (Knaflic) is about the decisions upstream of the plotting code: what to show, what to leave out, and how to structure a chart so the audience reaches the point you intended. Tool-agnostic, and the closest thing to a standard reference for the design side of @sec-comms-viz. The companion exercise book provides the practice.

## Modeling and Statistics

**[Tidy Modeling with R](https://www.tmwr.org/)** (Kuhn and Silge) is the companion book to the [tidymodels](https://www.tidymodels.org/) ecosystem, a collection of packages that bring tidyverse conventions to statistical modeling: splitting data, specifying model workflows, tuning hyperparameters, and evaluating performance. Tidymodels works with hundreds of model types through a consistent interface. The book and the tidymodels website are the primary resources for teams moving from exploratory analysis into predictive modeling.

## Public Health Data Science

**[The Epidemiologist R Handbook](https://epirhandbook.com/)** is a comprehensive, freely available reference manual written specifically for epidemiologists and public health practitioners using R. It covers data management, descriptive analyses, outbreak investigation, time series, spatial analysis, and reporting, with worked examples using realistic public health data. For DSTT teams, this is the most directly applicable reference for day-to-day analytical work.

**[Building Reproducible Analytical Pipelines with R](https://raps-with-r.dev/)** (Rodrigues) covers functional programming, package-based project structure, Docker, and Nix as a complete framework for building analyses that can be re-run reliably. It connects topics from the environments chapter (@sec-environments) and goes substantially deeper on each.

## Databases from R

Many agencies store surveillance data in relational databases such as SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Oracle, or SQLite. R can query these databases directly, returning results as data frames without any manual export step.

**[Posit's database guide](https://solutions.posit.co/connections/db/)** is the best starting point. It covers the overall architecture (DBI as the connection layer, specific driver packages per database type), connection setup in Positron and RStudio, and best practices for credentials and connection management.

**[DBI](https://dbi.r-dbi.org/)** is the foundational package. It defines the interface that all R database drivers implement: `dbConnect()` to open a connection, `dbGetQuery()` to run a SQL query and return results, `dbDisconnect()` to close the connection. If you know the SQL you want to run, DBI is the direct path.

**[dbplyr](https://dbplyr.tidyverse.org/)** extends dplyr to work against database tables. Instead of writing SQL, you write normal dplyr code (`filter()`, `mutate()`, `summarize()`) and dbplyr translates it to SQL and runs it on the database. This is useful when the team knows dplyr well and the database queries are not highly complex. `collect()` pulls the results into R as a local data frame.

## APIs and Public Data

**[httr2](https://httr2.r-lib.org/)** is the package for talking to web APIs from R, introduced in @sec-apis. Beyond the basics covered there, its documentation includes a "Wrapping APIs" vignette that walks through building a reusable interface to an API, useful if your team pulls from the same source in many projects.

**[Analyzing US Census Data](https://walker-data.com/census-r/)** (Walker) [@walker2023census] is the definitive guide to working with census data in R via the `tidycensus` package: ACS and decennial data, geography and mapping, and the margins-of-error handling that census estimates require. Freely available online. For public health teams, this is where rate denominators come from.

**[The Socrata developer documentation](https://dev.socrata.com/)** covers the API behind data.cdc.gov and many state open data portals, including the SoQL query language for filtering and aggregating on the server.

## Data Infrastructure

**[The DuckDB documentation](https://duckdb.org/docs/)** is unusually good, and the sections on reading Parquet, the CSV sniffer, and performance tuning cover most of what a public health team needs. [@raasveldt2019duckdb] is the original paper if you want the design rationale for columnar analytical engines, which is the background to @sec-infrastructure-olap.

**[MotherDuck](https://motherduck.com/docs/)** documents the hosted, shared version of DuckDB, which is the smallest step up from a local file when several people need to query the same data.

**[The FinOps Foundation](https://www.finops.org/introduction/what-is-finops/)** publishes vendor-neutral material on managing consumption-based cloud spend. Most of it is written for organizations far larger than a health department, and the core practices (attributing cost to a team, setting budgets with alerts, right-sizing compute) apply directly to the pricing problem described in @sec-infrastructure-pricing.

## BI Platforms

**[The Tableau REST API reference](https://help.tableau.com/current/api/rest_api/en-us/REST/rest_api.htm)** documents authentication, publishing, and extract refresh, which are the endpoints worth automating from R (@sec-bi-publishing). The vendor documentation is the only reliable source here, because these APIs version independently of any R wrapper.

**[The Power BI REST API reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/power-bi/)** covers dataset refresh and workspace management. The [Fabric REST API](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/rest/api/fabric/) documents additional Fabric services.

## Package Dependencies

**[Dependencies: Mindset and Background](https://r-pkgs.org/dependencies-mindset-background.html)** in *R Packages* explains the costs and benefits of package dependencies, complementing @sec-dependencies-cost.

**[The lifecycle package documentation](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html)** explains what each stage badge (stable, experimental, superseded, deprecated) commits a maintainer to, which is what you need to interpret a function's badge before building on it.

**[pak](https://pak.r-lib.org/)** installs packages and, more usefully here, shows dependency trees with `pkg_deps_tree()` before you commit to anything.

## Testing and Validation

**[The testthat documentation](https://testthat.r-lib.org/)** and the [testing chapters of *R Packages*](https://r-pkgs.org/testing-basics.html) [@wickham2023rpkgs] cover the framework introduced in @sec-testing, including test organization, fixtures, and snapshot testing.

**[pointblank](https://rstudio.github.io/pointblank/)** is the validation package used in @sec-validation. Its documentation covers agents, action levels, and the multi-agent reporting that makes validation results reviewable by non-programmers.

## Automation and Reproducible Environments

**[The targets user manual](https://books.ropensci.org/targets/)** [@landau2021targets] is the reference for the pipeline tool introduced in @sec-automation-targets. The chapters on debugging pipelines and branching over many inputs are useful for recurring surveillance work.

**[The Rocker Project](https://rocker-project.org/)** documents the Docker images used in @sec-environments-rocker, including which image to start from and how the versioned tags work.

**[renv documentation](https://rstudio.github.io/renv/)** covers lockfiles, restoring environments, and the cache, in more detail than @sec-environments-renv.

## Accessibility

**[The WCAG 2.2 quick reference](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/)** is the practical, filterable version of the standard behind the requirements in @sec-accessibility-regs. Filter to Level AA and to the guidelines relevant to your output type.

**[The Section508.gov training materials](https://www.section508.gov/training/)** are written for federal staff and cover documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.

## AI Tools and Governance

**[The NIST AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework)** [@nist2023airmf] and its companion playbook give an agency AI policy a structure that compliance reviewers recognize. The starting point for @sec-aigovernance-contents.

**[The OMB memoranda index](https://www.whitehouse.gov/omb/information-for-agencies/memoranda/)** is where current federal guidance on agency AI use lives. These are revised by administration, so check the index for current guidance.

**[The Posit Assistant documentation](https://positron.posit.co/assistant.html)** and the [Claude Code documentation](https://code.claude.com/docs/) cover the tools in @sec-ai in more depth than that chapter does, including configuration, permissions, and what context each tool sends.

## Team Practice and Onboarding

**[The GitLab Handbook](https://handbook.gitlab.com/)** documents how GitLab operates. Its scope exceeds a small epidemiology team's needs, but its structure and maintenance practices provide useful examples (@sec-onboarding-maintenance).

**[The Turing Way](https://book.the-turing-way.org/)** is a community-built guide to reproducible, ethical, collaborative data science. Its guides on project design, collaboration, and communication overlap substantially with the nontechnical part of this book and go deeper on several topics.

**[The Carpentries](https://carpentries.org/lessons/)** publish workshop curricula on R, the shell, Git, and SQL that a team can work through together. The lessons are openly licensed, so they can be adapted for your own onboarding material.

## Migrating from Legacy Tools

**[R for Excel Users](https://rstudio-conf-2020.github.io/r-for-excel/)** (Lowndes and Horst) is a free, workshop-format course aimed at analysts whose current workflow is Excel, covering the transition to R, RStudio, and reproducible project habits. A good group-study resource for teams working through the migration described in @sec-legacy.

**[haven](https://haven.tidyverse.org/)** reads SAS, SPSS, and Stata files into R, preserving value labels and special missing values. Its documentation covers the details of labelled data that matter when converting legacy datasets to open formats.

## Online Courses

The [**Johns Hopkins Data Science Specialization**](https://www.coursera.org/specializations/jhu-data-science) on Coursera is a 10-course sequence by Roger Peng, Jeff Leek, and Brian Caffo covering the complete applied data science workflow in R: tooling, data acquisition, exploratory analysis, reproducible research, statistical inference, regression, machine learning, and building data products. Check each course's current access options; preview, audit, and certificate terms vary. Public health practitioners may find these individual courses useful:

- [R Programming](https://www.coursera.org/learn/r-programming): the core language, data structures, control flow, and functions. A solid foundation if you are new to R or coming from another language.
- [Exploratory Data Analysis](https://www.coursera.org/learn/exploratory-data-analysis): visualization and summarization as an investigative tool, not a reporting tool.
- [Reproducible Research](https://www.coursera.org/learn/reproducible-research): the rationale and practice of literate programming in R, closely aligned with the approach in @sec-reporting.

The [**Johns Hopkins Executive Data Science Specialization**](https://www.coursera.org/specializations/executive-data-science) (also by Peng, Leek, and Caffo) is a shorter, less technical sequence aimed at managers who lead or commission data science work. It pairs well with @sec-pm and is useful for team leads who want to communicate more effectively with analysts.

## Version Control

**[Happy Git and GitHub for the useR](https://happygitwithr.com/)** (Bryan) is the companion reference to @sec-git. It covers installation and configuration in detail, the full range of workflows for collaborating on GitHub, and a substantial troubleshooting section for the inevitable moments when Git does something unexpected. Useful when you want to move beyond the introductory workflow.

## Quarto

The **[Quarto documentation](https://quarto.org/docs/guide/)** at quarto.org is comprehensive and well-maintained. Key sections beyond what this book covers:

- [Quarto Projects](https://quarto.org/docs/projects/quarto-projects.html): organizing multiple documents with shared configuration, a prerequisite for generating many parameterized reports at once.
- [GitHub Actions for Quarto](https://quarto.org/docs/publishing/github-pages.html#github-action): automating rendering and publishing on push, so reports update without manual intervention.
- [Quarto Extensions](https://quarto.org/docs/extensions/): community-contributed output formats, shortcodes, and filters that extend what Quarto can produce.
